title: Looped Transformers as Programmable Computers
relevance_reason: Canonical constructive result that a constant-depth transformer placed in a loop emulates a universal instruction-set computer.
one_sentence: Hand-constructs weights so that a looped encoder transformer of at most 13 layers executes SUBLEQ/FLEQ programs from a punchcard-style input (instructions, memory, scratchpad), emulating a calculator, linear algebra routines and in-context SGD.
key_contributions: Attention/MLP gadgets for read, write, program counter, conditional branch and function calls; a 9-layer, 2-head looped transformer of width O(log n + N) runs SUBLEQ programs (Turing complete given unbounded memory).
Generalized FLEQ instruction with M function blocks: depth 9 + max_i l_i, dimensionality O(Md + log n), one instruction per loop.
13-layer looped constructions for matrix inversion (Newton), power iteration and T iterations of SGD on a two-layer network (in-context learning).

setup.model_sizes: 9 layers/2 heads (SUBLEQ); 13 layers/1 head (matrix inversion, power iteration, SGD); width O(log n + N) or O(log n + d)
setup.loops_test: one loop per executed instruction (T loops for T instructions)

claims.claim: Lemma 4: a 9-layer, 2-head looped transformer with width O(log n + N) (n = program+memory length, N = bits per integer) executes SUBLEQ programs; SUBLEQ is Turing complete given infinite memory.
claims.evidence_quote: There exists a looped transformer architecture that can run SUBLEQ programs. This architecture has nine layers, two heads, and a width of O(log(n) + N )

claims.claim: Theorem 2: with M transformer function blocks, a looped transformer of depth 9 + max l_i, sum of heads, dimensionality O(Md + log n) run T times executes T FLEQ instructions (mem[c] = f_m(mem[a], mem[b]); conditional goto).
claims.evidence_quote: dimensionality O(M d + log n) such that running it recurrently T times can run T instructions of any program where each instruction is FLEQ

claims.claim: The loop is what keeps depth independent of program length; total runtime still scales with program length as expected from circuit-depth considerations.
claims.evidence_quote: Note however that the depth of the looped transfromer itself does not scale with the size of the program.

claims.claim: Lemma 15: a 13-layer, 1-head looped transformer of dimensionality O(log D + d) implements T iterations of SGD on a two-layer network over D in-context points, up to error epsilon.
claims.evidence_quote: there exists a transformer with 13 layers, 1 head and dimensionality O(log(D) + d) that uses the Unified Attention Based Computer framework in Section 5.2 to implement T iterations of SGD on a two layer neural network

numbers.quote: There exists a looped transformer with less than 13 layers that can emulate a general purpose computer (see Sec. 5), a basic calculator (see Sec. 7)
the width of the transformer scales logarithmically with the length of the program, and memory used. This is a side-effect of the bit-complexity of our positional encodings

limitations: Pure existence constructions with hand-set weights; softmax approximates hardmax via temperature so errors must be controlled; width grows with log of program/memory length; inputs are embedding vectors not tokens/natural language; no training or learnability; authors list experimental validation and training of such networks as open problems.
builds_on: Pérez et al. (Attention is Turing complete)
survey_notes: Anchor for 'expressivity and universality'. Universality here is via an external loop over a fixed-length sequence that holds program + memory; memory is bounded by sequence length n (Turing completeness needs unbounded memory), so it is a constant-depth, fixed-width per n machine whose state is the whole sequence (a 'full sequence-state loop' in the language of 2605.30757). Explicitly cautions that constructions share no similarity with how real LMs are trained. Basis for later work: 2410.09375 (looped ReLU MLPs), 2604.08816 (Loom, C programs in 8 layers), 2502.17416 (cites as Turing-machine simulation). No empirical test at LM scale.

title: Looped Transformers for Length Generalization
relevance_reason: Defines n-RASP-L task class and shows weight-tied looped decoders with step-dependent supervision and adaptive loop count length-generalize.
one_sentence: Defines n-RASP-L (tasks solvable by T(n) iterations of a RASP-L step), trains a looped NoPE decoder with input injection supervised only on the final answer after T(n) loops, and shows strong length generalization with oracle or max-confidence stopping.
key_contributions: n-RASP-L definition with explicit n-RASP-L programs for parity (T(n)=n), copy (T(n)=n) and binary addition (T(n)=n+1).
Training scheme: full-output prediction (FOP), input injection, NoPE, loss on final output after the sample-specific number of loops T(n) (no intermediate supervision).
Adaptive inference via oracle step count or max-confidence (min cross-entropy over steps) stopping; beats NTP, NTP-pause and fixed-depth weight-tied NTP-Loop baselines.

setup.model_sizes: GPT-2 decoder block with NoPE, 256 embedding dims, block depth 1-4 layers, 8-64 heads (task-specific)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: online i.i.d. sampled synthetic data, 100k gradient steps, batch 64, curriculum over length; training lengths [1,20) for most tasks, [1,12) for multiplication
setup.loops_train: T(n) loops per sample (e.g. T = n for parity/copy, n+1 for addition, product of lengths for multiplication)
setup.loops_test: T(n') with oracle, or argmin-loss step up to T_max (max-confidence)
setup.baselines: vanilla NTP with depth 20x the looped block; NTP with pause tokens; NTP-Loop (weight-tied, fixed 20 steps); FOP, FOP-Pause, looped without input injection
setup.benchmarks: Parity, Copy (repeated tokens), Binary Addition, Binary Sum, Binary Multiplication, Unique Set

claims.claim: Looped transformers with step-dependent final-answer supervision and adaptive loop count length-generalize far beyond training length (parity: trained to 20 digits, near-perfect at 40+).
claims.regime: iso_data; NTP baseline depth matched to 20 loops (iso_effective_depth during training)
claims.evidence_quote: For example, for Parity, it can generalize to more than 40 digits near perfectly when trained with up to 20 digits.

claims.claim: Fixed-depth weight tying (NTP-Loop) and pause tokens help somewhat but are clearly worse than adaptive depth; pause tokens add parallel not sequential compute.
claims.evidence_quote: Variants of NTP could improve generalization but not as effectively as our adaptive-depth model.

claims.claim: Input injection improves length generalization, most visibly on addition, binary sum and unique set.
claims.evidence_quote: The effect of input injection is more visible in tasks like Addition, Binary Sum, and Unique Set.

claims.claim: Max-confidence stopping (lowest cross-entropy over steps) selects near-perfect steps; on several tasks the model converges (stays correct) after solving although never trained to converge, which makes per-sample stopping work.
claims.evidence_quote: the looped model somehow learns to converge for a certain number of steps after solving the task, even though we do not explicitly train the model to converge

claims.claim: Propositions 3.2-3.4: parity, copy and n-digit binary addition admit n-RASP-L programs with T(n)=n, n, n+1 iterations of a fixed RASP-L step.
claims.evidence_quote: There exists a n-RASP-L program with T (n) = n + 1 that solves the n-digit addition task

numbers.what: NTP baseline depth relative to looped block
numbers.quote: we train the transformer model with a depth 20 times the depth of the looped block in our approach
We use the decoder-only GPT-2 model with NoPE and 256 embedding dimensions as the basic block for the looped iterations
with batch size 64, and train for a total number of 100k gradient steps
we test with 6400 random samples in Figure 4, 5, 7, 6, and report the mean exact match accuracy and standard error from five training runs with different random seeds

limitations: Requires ground-truth step count T(n) at training time; n-RASP-L covers only single-loop programs; full BPTT through many loops is expensive; small models and short lengths only; NoPE only; inference slightly costlier than fixed-depth baselines.
venue: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025
builds_on: 2311.12424 (Yang et al., looped TF learn learning algorithms)
survey_notes: Anchor for 'length generalization: what makes extrapolation work'. Three ingredients: input injection, loop count tied to problem size during training (step-dependent supervision), adaptive stopping. Agrees with 2202.05826 (recall = input injection; progressive training) on algorithmic extrapolation. Contrasts with McLeish et al. (2405.17399, cited footnote 8) who did not find adaptive depth helpful with fixed-depth weight tying. Later 2606.29983 argues the length-loop coupling used here creates a spurious correlation that inflates OOD variance and proposes stochastic loop counts. Not tested at LM scale.

title: End-to-end Algorithm Synthesis with Recurrent Networks: Logical Extrapolation Without Overthinking
relevance_reason: Lineage paper for recurrent-depth extrapolation: weight-tied conv block iterated more at test time; introduces recall (input injection) and progressive loss.
one_sentence: Weight-tied recurrent ResNet blocks with recall (input concatenated at every iteration) and a progressive loss (random detached prefix, random extra iterations) extrapolate from small training problems to far larger ones without degrading as iterations grow.
key_contributions: Recall architecture: concatenate the raw input to the features entering the recurrent block at every iteration (an early form of input injection).
Incremental progress training: run n ~ U{0,m-1} iterations without gradients, then train k ~ U{1,m-n} more iterations, mixed with the full m-iteration loss; discourages iteration counting.
Identifies 'overthinking' (accuracy collapse with many test iterations) and shows recall + progressive loss yield fixed-point-like, non-degrading behavior up to thousands of iterations.

setup.model_sizes: fully convolutional DT nets; width 400 filters (prefix sums), 512 filters (chess); recurrent block = one four-layer residual block
setup.train_tokens_or_data: easy-to-hard-data: 32-bit prefix sums, 9x9 mazes, first 600K easiest chess puzzles
setup.loops_train: m = 30 maximum iterations
setup.loops_test: up to hundreds (prefix sums 512-bit), 2,000 (201x201 mazes) and 20,000 (801x801 mazes)
setup.baselines: DT without recall/progressive loss; feed-forward ResNets of the same effective depth as 30-iteration DT
setup.benchmarks: prefix sums mod 2, mazes, chess puzzles

claims.claim: Without recall and progressive loss, DT networks get 0% on 512-bit prefix sums after training on 32-bit strings; DT-Recall with progressive loss solves more than 97%.
claims.evidence_quote: DT networks are unable to solve very long binary strings, achieving 0% accuracy on 512-bit data, while DT-Recall models with progressive loss can solve more than 97% after approximately 200 iterations

claims.claim: Trained on 9x9 mazes, DT-Recall with progressive loss solves 74% of 201x201 mazes; feed-forward and prior DT systems completely fail on 59x59.
claims.regime: iso_effective_depth (FF ResNet of same depth as 30-iteration DT) and iso_data
claims.evidence_quote: we can push these systems to their limits (and the limits of our hardware) and find that our models can solve 74% of the 201 × 201 mazes

claims.claim: Recall is what prevents overthinking; recalled models appear to converge to a fixed point rather than becoming unstable as iterations grow.
claims.evidence_quote: the overthinking problem often seems to disappear when skip connections are added to provide networks with an uninterrupted view of the input

claims.claim: Random starting iteration n in progressive training matters: n=0 gives 90.27% vs 97.12% with random n on 512-bit prefix sums.
claims.evidence_quote: DT networks with recall on average solve 90.27% of 512-bit test samples when trained with the n = 0 loss, and with randomly sampled values of n, as described in Algorithm 1, they achieve 97.12% accuracy

numbers.what: 59x59 maze accuracy, DT-Recall with progressive loss
numbers.quote: highlighted by the fact that DT-Recall models with progressive loss achieve on average 97%

numbers.what: 59x59 maze accuracy, DT-Recall without progressive loss
numbers.quote: accuracy while DT-Recall models without progressive loss only reach an average of 83%

numbers.value: 2,000 and 20,000 iterations (10,004 and 100,004 conv layers equivalent)
numbers.quote: which our models solve using 2,000 and 20,000 iterations, respectively (the equivalent of 10,004 and 100,004 convolutional layers in depth)
In Figure 5, we see that our techniques lead to a 4% accuracy improvement compared to networks without them.
We train our models on 32-bit strings with a maximum of only m = 30 recurrent iterations

limitations: Convolutional models on grid/string tasks with input-shaped outputs, not language models; best progressive-loss weight alpha is task dependent (1, 0.01, 0.5); no theoretical guarantees.
venue: 36th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2022).
survey_notes: Origin of two design choices that recur in looped LMs: input re-injection ('recall', cf. Huginn, 2409.15647 input injection) and randomized/truncated unroll training (cf. Huginn's randomized recurrence, 2606.29983 stochastic loop counts). 'Overthinking' (degradation past training horizon) is the empirical failure mode later analyzed dynamically by 2608.18222 (settling vs drifting operators) and 2410.03020 (mazes, implicit networks). Not language; no LM-scale test.

title: Chain-of-Thought and Compressed Looped Transformers: A Memory-Budget Separation
relevance_reason: Formal comparison of looped transformers vs CoT via persistent mutable memory; conditional separation for compressed-state loops.
one_sentence: Defines compressed latent loops (s persistent slots), sequence-state loops (n positions) and CoT scratchpads by persistent mutable memory; proves compressed loops lie in DSPACE(sdp + log n + log T), so polylog-state loops cannot decide P-complete problems unless P is in polylog space, while polynomial CoT can.
key_contributions: Memory accounting: compressed latent loop M = s d p, sequence-state loop M = n d p, CoT M = Theta(l log|Sigma|).

Theorem 4.2: CLL[s,d,p,T] in DSPACE(O(sdp + log n + log T)) under log precision and logspace uniformity; Theorem 4.4: conditional separation from polynomial-length CoT on P-complete problems; Proposition 4.3: sequence-state loops are memory-rich (linear space) and escape the bound.
Finite-size probes: k-chain pointer chasing collapses when slots s < k; gated linear attention associative recall needs state dimension growing with number of pairs.

setup.model_sizes: small synthetic models (pointer chasing on n = 16 cells; associative recall with gated linear attention)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: synthetic pointer-chasing and associative-recall data
setup.loops_train: T = 16 iterations (pointer chasing)
setup.baselines: sequence-state loop (SSL) control; full softmax attention and vanilla linear attention controls for recall
setup.benchmarks: k-concurrent pointer chasing (k in {1,2,4,8}, s in {1,2,4,8,16}); associative recall with N in {8,16,24} pairs, state dimension m from 4 to 128

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2: a compressed latent loop with s slots, width d, precision p, T iterations (log precision, logspace-uniform) is simulable in deterministic space O(sdp + log n + log T); with polylog state and quasi-polynomial T it is a polylog-space machine.
claims.evidence_quote: In particular, if s d p = polylog(n) and log T = polylog(n) (e.g. for polynomially many iterations), then CLL ⊆ DSPACE(polylogn).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4: assuming P is not contained in DSPACE(polylog n), no logspace-uniform compressed loop with polylog persistent state and log T = polylog(n) decides a P-complete language, whereas polynomial-length CoT can.
claims.evidence_quote: Under a standard complexity assumption, such loops cannot decide problems that are P-complete under logspace reductions, whereas polynomiallength chain-of-thought can.

claims.claim: The separation does not apply to standard looped transformers that carry a hidden vector at every position (sequence-state loops) or that append padding/scratch positions; these are memory-rich, consistent with prior universality and CoT-simulation results.
claims.evidence_quote: The separation is specific to compressed loops, as full sequence-state loops carry state at every input position and live in a memory-rich regime closer to explicit scratchpads.

claims.claim: Finite-size probe: in k-concurrent pointer chasing, compressed loops with fewer slots than chains (s < k) collapse while the sequence-state control is essentially saturated; above threshold, success is seed-dependent.
claims.regime: not_applicable (controlled sweep, recurrence depth and training fixed)
claims.evidence_quote: In the subdiagonal regime s < k the collapse is robust, with mean cell accuracy 0.041 and maximum cell-mean 0.129.

numbers.what: SSL control accuracy on pointer chasing k = 2,4,8
numbers.quote: The sequence-state control is essentially saturated, reaching 0.999 mean accuracy for k = 2, 4, 8

numbers.what: associative recall critical state dimension m_crit (median, range)
numbers.quote: N =8 has median 8 and range 4 to 16, N =16 has median 32 and range 16 to 64, and N =24 has median 64 and range 32 to 128
sweeping s ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} and k ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8}, T = 16 iterations, ten seeds

limitations: Asymptotic and conditional on P not in DSPACE(polylog n); log-precision logspace-uniform model; no lower bound for sequence-state loops, padded loops, stochastic decoding or growing-state architectures; experiments are finite-size probes not tests of the theorem; practical looped LMs sit between the s d p and n d p regimes.
survey_notes: Key for the survey's 'memory as a third resource' framing: depth (loops) buys time, not persistent memory; CoT buys both. Reconciles apparently opposite results: looped>=CoT simulations (2502.17416 Thm 5.4, 2509.25239 parallel advantage) all concern sequence-state loops; the negative result concerns compressed loops only. Practical looped LMs (Huginn, Ouro) are sequence-state loops with KV caches, so the theorem does not directly constrain them; it constrains latent-slot / pooled / low-rank-state designs. Untested at LM scale; authors propose exposing a persistent-state knob as an experimental target. Single-author preprint, no venue.

title: Exploration of Fast-Slow Latent Recurrence for Train-Short, Test-Long Generalization
relevance_reason: Weight-shared inner depth loop per observation inside a persistent stream-level recurrence; looped depth applied to streaming rather than a static input.
one_sentence: Applies T weight-shared latent updates of a recurrent core per observation and carries the latent across stream steps without reset; trained on short streams it extrapolates far longer (Dyck, mazes, Minigrid) than RNN, SSM, Transformer and Looped-TF baselines.
key_contributions: Persistent fast-slow formulation Z_s(t+1) = R(Z_s(t), C_s), Z_{s+1}(0) = Z_s(T): reduces to an RNN at T=1, a weight-tied deep-transition RNN for T>1.
Ablations: OOD accuracy grows with inner iterations T then saturates; weight sharing beats an unshared stack with more parameters.
Core ablation: state-dependent token mixing and feature-wise nonlinear mixing are the ingredients associated with OOD generalization (LSTM+FFN core competitive with attention cores).

setup.model_sizes: small task models (parameter counts in appendix Tables 4 and 6); Qwen3-4B-Base fine-tuned as a baseline
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Dyck-(30,5) trained up to length 40; Local-Maze small mazes; Minigrid via PPO
setup.loops_train: T inner iterations per observation (swept 1 to 16 on Local-Maze)
setup.loops_test: same T (test-time T sweep in appendix)
setup.baselines: LSTM, Mamba2/S5, DeltaProduct, TransformerXL, Transformer, Looped TF (2409.15647), CTM, prompted frontier LLMs, fine-tuned Qwen3-4B-Base
setup.benchmarks: Dyck-(30,5), Local-Maze navigation, Minigrid (LavaCrossing, DoorKey, MultiRoom)

claims.claim: Trained on Dyck sequences up to length 40, FSRM keeps about 80% token accuracy up to length 10^5, three orders of magnitude beyond training.
claims.evidence_quote: our model of this family, trained on sequences of length ≤ 40, maintains ≈ 80% token accuracy up to length 105 , three orders of magnitude beyond training

claims.claim: Weight sharing in the inner loop matters: at the same inner budget T=5 the shared loop beats an unshared 5-layer stack with about twice the parameters, and a 10-layer stack is worse still.
claims.regime: iso_effective_depth (stack L⊗1 vs loop 1⊗T) and iso_param (loop vs base)
claims.evidence_quote: With the same inner-loop budget (T = 5), the shared recurrent loop reaches roughly 61% OOD accuracy, whereas the unshared 5-layer stack drops to about 51%, despite using roughly twice as many parameters.

claims.claim: Static-input looped models without the persistent fast-slow mechanism, including looped Transformers, do not show the OOD generalization.
claims.evidence_quote: models without this persistent fast–slow mechanism, including looped Transformers, do not exhibit OOD generalization

numbers.quote: but still falls to the chance rate of approximately 50% at length 20,480, roughly an order of magnitude shorter than the horizon at which FSRM maintains high accuracy

limitations: Trades parallelism for expressivity (inner loop per observation, slow inference without specialized kernels); restricted to tasks with compact stream-level structure; inner-loop count fixed, no adaptive halting.
survey_notes: Belongs at the boundary of 'length generalization' and 'sequence-axis recurrence': inner depth loop per token with persistent state, akin to deep-transition RNNs. Iso-param/iso-depth table (Table 2) reproduces the Saunshi (2502.17416) (k⊗L) vs (kL⊗1) design for an OOD metric and finds looping beats unshared depth, which agrees in direction with 2502.17416 reasoning results. Contrast with 2605.30757: FSRM is a compressed-state recurrent model (bounded memory), suited to finite-state tasks like bounded-depth Dyck, which is consistent with the memory-budget view. Comparisons to frontier LLMs are unmatched.

title: DART: Distributional Adversarial Recurrent Training for Algorithm Learning
relevance_reason: Training objective for weight-tied recurrent reasoning models (Deep Thinking, TRM) aimed at easy-to-hard extrapolation and stable iteration; not an LM.
one_sentence: Replaces one-hot instance supervision for recurrent reasoning models with a noise-softened local target distribution matched via a WGAN-style critic; improves easy-to-hard extrapolation and iteration stability of Deep Thinking nets and TRM on mazes, chess and masked Sudoku.
key_contributions: Frames easy-to-hard failure as solution-space imbalance: invalid solutions grow much faster than valid ones with difficulty.
DART: supervised loss plus adversarial alignment to a local soft target around the ground truth, applicable to DT-Recall and TRM.
Shows DART is complementary to progressive training (2202.05826): DART raises solution quality, progressive training fixes late-iteration overthinking.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: 9x9 mazes; easiest 500K chess puzzles; Sudoku-Extreme with 20% masking
setup.loops_test: up to iteration 50 on chess; computation depth up to 56 on Sudoku (TRM)
setup.baselines: cross-entropy (CE) training, progressive training, label smoothing, Gaussian softened targets
setup.benchmarks: Maze (13x13, 31x31 test), Chess puzzles (indices 600K-700K test), Sudoku-Extreme with 30/40/50% masking

claims.claim: On 31x31 mazes (trained on 9x9), CE training is unstable across seeds while DART reaches near-perfect peak and final accuracy.
claims.regime: iso_param, iso_data (same architecture and data, different objective)
claims.evidence_quote: DART removes most of this sensitivity, reaching 99.91 ± 0.13% peak and final accuracy at 31 × 31.

claims.claim: On chess, CE peaks then collapses with more iterations (overthinking); progressive training removes the collapse and progressive DART gives the best final accuracy, so the two address complementary failure modes.
claims.evidence_quote: Progressive DART inherits the same long-horizon stability while retaining a distributional objective, achieving the best final accuracy, 83.52 ± 0.16%.

claims.claim: For TRM on Sudoku trained with 20% masking, DART's gain over CE grows with the distribution shift.
claims.evidence_quote: at depth 56, the gain is 0.5% at 30% masking, 3.3% at 40%, and 5.6% at 50%

numbers.quote: CE reaches only 73.92 ± 26.01% peak accuracy, with a bimodal outcome across seeds
CE reaches a moderate peak of 80.81 ± 0.37% (Table 4), but by iteration 50 collapses to 0.92 ± 0.08%.

limitations: Evaluated only on Maze, Chess and masked Sudoku with DTS and TRM; DART alone does not remove late-iteration overthinking on chess; benefits of target softening alone are task dependent.
survey_notes: Training-objective lever for extrapolation in recurrent reasoners, orthogonal to architecture. Confirms overthinking (accuracy collapse past training horizon) persists in DT models without progressive training, consistent with 2202.05826 and the drifting-operator analysis in 2608.18222. Not language; small models.

title: Loom: A Scalable Analytical Neural Computer Architecture
relevance_reason: Constructive (hand-weighted) looped transformer computer extending Giannou et al.; no learning, no language.
one_sentence: Builds an 8-layer looped transformer with analytically derived, program-independent weights that executes a 22-opcode ISA compiled from C, one instruction per forward pass, halting when the program counter reaches zero.
key_contributions: 22-opcode ISA (SUBLEQ plus 21 extended opcodes) in 8 layers via opcode-as-operand-routing to a single shared subtract core and single-layer direct subtraction.
Fixed-size state tensor X in R^{d x n} holds scratchpad, memory and instructions; same weights run any compiled program; L8 snaps state back to {-1,+1} to remove floating-point drift between loops.
C compiler (Python/JS), demos (sorting, Snake, raycasting, 9x9 Sudoku in 284 instructions) and FPGA synthesis with argmax attention.

setup.model_sizes: d=155, n=1024: 4.7M parameters, 928 instruction slots (default); 146x512 compact; 164x2048 large
setup.loops_test: one forward pass per instruction until PC = 0
setup.baselines: Giannou et al. 2301.13196 SUBLEQ construction
setup.benchmarks: 42 opcode tests, 19 cross-head writeback tests, 50 compiled-C tests

claims.claim: A fixed-weight 8-layer transformer, iterated, executes any program compiled from a C subset to a 22-opcode ISA, with fixed per-step cost independent of program length or history.
claims.evidence_quote: The full machine state resides in a single tensor X ∈ Rd×n of fixed size, and every step has fixed cost for fixed d and n, independent of program length or execution history.

claims.claim: Extends Giannou et al. from one opcode to 22 opcodes while reducing depth.
claims.evidence_quote: Their construction uses 10 transformer layers for this single instruction. We extend this result from 1 opcode in 10 layers to 22 opcodes in 8 layers.

claims.claim: All compiled-program correctness tests pass and match an independent ISA interpreter.
claims.evidence_quote: We ran 50 end-to-end compiled-program tests including Fibonacci, GCD by subtraction, array minimum, nested conditionals, variable-index LOAD/STORE round-trips, and multi-iteration loops (up to 1000 ISA steps). All 50 tests pass.

numbers.quote: The default configuration uses d = 155 and n = 1024, yielding 4.7 million parameters and 928 instruction slots.
Adding STORE reduces the 9×9 Sudoku solver from 1,085 to 284 instructions
yielding approximately 0.3 seconds per transformer step. For comparison, the same model runs at ∼10 ms/step on an NVIDIA RTX 4080 via ONNX Runtime WebGPU.

limitations: Hand-constructed weights, no learning; memory bounded by n columns; relies on high softmax temperature (effectively hard attention) and per-step error correction; FPGA implementation is slow (sequential column processing).
survey_notes: Engineering continuation of 2301.13196 in the 'expressivity/universality' subsection: shows constant-depth looped transformers as practical fixed-state computers. Minor factual discrepancy: Loom says Giannou et al. used 10 layers for SUBLEQ, whereas 2301.13196 Lemma 4 states nine layers. State is a fixed d x n tensor (sequence-state loop in 2605.30757's terms), so memory is bounded by n. Nothing to test at LM scale.

title: Statistical Gains from Looped Estimation under Parameter Budgets
relevance_reason: First statistical risk separation between looped (shared-parameter) and untied networks/Transformers under a common parameter budget.
one_sentence: Proves that looped residual FFNs and post-LN Transformers with a fixed number of bounded parameters reach the Hölder minimax rate (up to logs) by growing iterations, while any untied estimator under the same parameter budget keeps risk bounded away from zero.
key_contributions: Upper squared-Hellinger risk bound for looped sieve MLE: approximation term ~ (log(eBT)/(BT))^a and estimation term ~ B(log(en) + T log(eB))/n, with a = 2s/d; minimax lower bound for the jointly tuned untied family ~ (B^2 log(eB))^{-a}.

Theorem 4.4 (fixed budget): with T_n ~ n^{1/(a+1)}, looped risk vanishes while untied risk stays positive, so the ratio tends to 0; Theorem 4.5 extends to growing budgets B_n ~ n^{gamma_B} with gamma_B < d/(4s+2d).
Numerical studies (residual FFNs only; Transformer results theoretical) in regression, energy-based density estimation and real-data prediction.

setup.model_sizes: parameter cap B (e.g. B = 128 in regression simulations)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: synthetic regression (bumps, recurrence, Friedman1), energy-based density estimation, real-data prediction
setup.loops_train: T_n growing with sample size in theory; fixed T in sample-size experiments
setup.baselines: Single (T=1) and Untied residual FFNs under the same parameter cap
setup.benchmarks: MSE, predictive log loss, squared Hellinger distance

claims.claim: At a sufficiently large fixed budget, the looped estimator's worst-case risk vanishes as n grows, whereas every estimator in the untied family under the same budget has risk bounded away from zero.
claims.regime: iso_param (common budget of distinct trainable coefficients); compute not matched
claims.evidence_quote: At sufficiently large fixed budgets, looped worst-case risk vanishes while optimal worst-case untied risk remains bounded away from zero.

claims.claim: Looped residual FFNs and post-LN Transformers attain the minimax polynomial rate for Hölder targets up to log factors with a fixed number of bounded real parameters.
claims.evidence_quote: looped residual feedforward networks and postlayer-normalized Transformers attain the minimax polynomial rate up to logarithmic factors with a fixed number of bounded real parameters

claims.claim: More loops trade approximation error for estimation complexity: iterations improve the approximation bound without adding parameters but increase computation and fitted-class complexity; the separation regime needs T_n/B_n to infinity, i.e. much more compute than the untied stack.
claims.evidence_quote: In the separation regime, Tn /Bn → ∞, whereas untied depth is at most O(Bn ); a dense residual FFN loop uses order Bn Tn parameter-associated operations per forward pass

claims.claim: Empirically at cap B = 128, the looped residual FFN has the smallest mean regression MSE on all three synthetic families.
claims.evidence_quote: At the prespecified cap B = 128, Loop has the smallest mean MSE for all three families (Table S1).

numbers.what: largest relative MSE reduction of Loop (recurrence target)
numbers.quote: The largest relative reductions occur for the recurrence: 46.5% against Single and 70.4% against Untied.

limitations: Worst-case risk of exact/approximate sieve MLE, not of SGD-trained models; optimization difficulty of shared parameters left open; constructions need increasingly precise coefficient encodings and growing intermediate magnitudes (precision not budgeted); Transformer analysis limited to one softmax head, post-LN, specific inputs; Transformer results not tested empirically.
survey_notes: Only statistical-learning (sample-complexity) result in my list: it formalizes the parameter axis of the survey thesis (looping buys accuracy per parameter, paid in compute). The comparison is strictly iso-parameter and explicitly not iso-compute (loop uses ~B*T ops vs ~B for untied), which matches the empirical iso-param framing of 2502.17416; it says nothing about iso-FLOP comparisons. Numerical evidence only on small residual FFNs; LM-scale prediction untested.

title: Universal Transformers for Circuit Computations: Perfect Length Generalization in Tiny Transformers
relevance_reason: Provably correct single-layer Universal (looped) Transformer with autonomous halting that evaluates arbitrary-depth circuits; learnable from depth 1-2 data.
one_sentence: Hand-constructs (and then learns from random init) a tiny single-layer looped transformer with a depth-tracking positional gating and masked hard attention that reduces circuit depth by one per iteration and halts after d iterations, giving perfect length generalization on Boolean, modular arithmetic and ListOps.
key_contributions: Theorem 1: one iteration (PE gating, attention, MLP, gated residual) evaluates every reducible depth-1 subexpression and reduces active depth by one; Theorem 2: after d(x) iterations the state equals the expression's value, with autonomous halting; O(n) per iteration via linear attention, O(n d) total.
Learnability: random-init models trained on depth 1-2 snap to exact solutions (10/10 seeds arithmetic, 9/10 Boolean and ListOps) and reach 100% accuracy at depths 3-30 (up to ~41k tokens).
Standard looped transformer (2409.15647 style) with learned PE, RoPE or FIRE under the same protocol collapses toward chance beyond training depth.

setup.model_sizes: 924 (arithmetic), 280 (Boolean), 4416 (ListOps) parameters
setup.train_tokens_or_data: fully parenthesized expressions of depth 1 and 2
setup.loops_train: number of iterations equals problem depth
setup.loops_test: autonomous halting after d iterations, depth 3-30
setup.baselines: standard looped transformer with learned PE / RoPE / FIRE (ground-truth depth supplied), CRvNN
setup.benchmarks: Boolean expressions, modular arithmetic (mod 10), ListOps

claims.claim: Theorems 1-2: the constructed single-layer looped transformer evaluates any valid fully-parenthesized Boolean expression of depth d exactly in d iterations and halts autonomously.
claims.evidence_quote: Combined with an autonomous halting criterion, the model terminates after d iterations for problems of depth d, yielding O(n · d) total complexity.

claims.claim: Trained from random initialization on depth 1-2 only, the architecture reaches 100% accuracy at every test depth from 3 to 30.
claims.evidence_quote: We achieved 100% generalization accuracy on all 3 tasks by training models from random initialization on depth 1 and 2 problems, and evaluating 100 problems at each depth from 3-30.

claims.claim: A standard weight-shared looped transformer with learned, RoPE or FIRE positional encodings, given the ground-truth depth, fits training depths but collapses toward chance out of distribution.
claims.regime: iso_data (same protocol, iteration count and hyperparameters); not iso-param
claims.evidence_quote: Every trained model still collapses toward chance out of distribution, whereas our construction remains exact.

numbers.quote: We limited evaluation to problems with up to depth 30 due to memory limitations (depth 30 ListOps problems had upwards of 41k tokens).

numbers.value: 0.67 at depth 3 to 0.17 at depth 10, ~500x more parameters
numbers.quote: despite roughly 500× more parameters, it degrades from 0.67 at depth 3 to 0.17 at depth 10 despite fitting the training depths

limitations: Requires fully parenthesized well-formed inputs (structure explicit in the string); local reductions cannot handle global sequential dependencies like long carry; fan-in <= 3; exactness relies on hardmax masking, straight-through discretization and deterministic halting.
survey_notes: Shows that the decisive ingredient for perfect depth extrapolation here is a task-structured positional encoding plus hard masking and halting, not looping per se: a plain looped transformer (2409.15647 recipe, oracle depth) collapses out of distribution on these circuit tasks. This qualifies 2409.15647's results (which were on n-RASP-L tasks with NoPE and FOP). The circuit-reduction procedure needs only depth-many iterations, matching the 'log-depth / depth-proportional' expressivity story (2502.17416 group composition in log n loops). Code mentioned as available but no URL found in text.

title: Stabilizing Extrapolation in Looped Transformers via Learned Stochastic Stopping
relevance_reason: Controlled study of loop-count schedules during training of looped transformers for length generalization; stochastic and RL-learned stopping.
one_sentence: Shows looped transformers trained with deterministic loop counts (fixed or length-matched, as in 2409.15647) contain extrapolating solutions but select them unreliably across runs; randomizing the training loop count, or learning it with REINFORCE (RL-Halting), sharply reduces OOD variance.
key_contributions: Extrapolation-stability gap: deterministic looped models have high run-to-run OOD variance (std 0.087 at K=20, 0.122 at K=n vs <= 0.009 for fixed-depth transformers); larger loop budgets increase both potential and variance.
Stochastic schedules K = clip(n + Delta) stabilize predictions across inference-time loop counts (lower flip rate) and across runs; toy gradient-averaging explanation.
RL-Halting learned stopping distribution gives best OOD accuracy and lowest std on addition, Dyck-1, Unique Set but can stabilize a suboptimal computation (Copy).

setup.model_sizes: shared 3-layer block (looped); 3-layer and 60-layer fixed-depth transformer baselines
setup.train_tokens_or_data: synthetic, lengths n < 20
setup.loops_train: fixed K=20, length-matched K=n, randomized K=clip(n+Delta) with window +-1/5/10, or RL-learned
setup.loops_test: sweep of K; OOD lengths 20-60
setup.baselines: 3-layer transformer (param-matched to one looped block), 60-layer transformer (higher compute), PonderNet-style baseline (appendix)
setup.benchmarks: binary addition, Dyck-1, Unique Set, Copy

claims.claim: Looped transformers show extrapolation potential on binary addition but it is unreliable: runs with similar ID accuracy diverge OOD, with much larger variance than fixed-depth transformers.
claims.evidence_quote: the OOD standard deviation is only 0.009 and 0.005 for the 3-layer and 60-layer Transformer baselines, but rises to 0.087 for Looped Transformers with fixed K = 20 and 0.122 for Looped Transformers with K = n

claims.claim: The variance is traced to the spurious correlation between sequence length and number of loops; randomizing loop count during training reduces OOD variance and stabilizes predictions across inference-time loop counts.
claims.evidence_quote: We trace this variance to the spurious correlation in simple algorithmic tasks between sequence length and number of loops.

claims.claim: Stochastic schedules stabilize rather than monotonically improve accuracy: OOD accuracy improves from deterministic to +-5 window but decreases at +-10.
claims.evidence_quote: Central OOD performance improves from the deterministic schedule to the ±5 window, but decreases again for the ±10 window.

claims.claim: RL-Halting gives best OOD accuracy and lowest std on three of four tasks, but on Copy it stabilizes a worse computation.
claims.evidence_quote: Across binary addition, Dyck-1, Unique Set, and Copy, learned stochastic stopping often improves this trade-off but can also stabilize a suboptimal computation.

limitations: Small synthetic tasks only; evaluation primarily via oracle-over-iterations accuracy (uses ground truth to pick depth); stabilization does not guarantee extrapolation; learned stopping can lock in a suboptimal computation.
survey_notes: Directly qualifies 2409.15647: the length-matched (K = n) schedule that 2409.15647 relies on produces high run-to-run OOD variance; 2409.15647 reported mean of 5 seeds. Agrees with 2202.05826 (randomized iteration counts in progressive training) and Huginn's randomized-recurrence training as a stabilizer. Message for the survey: loop-count policy at training time is a design axis affecting which algorithm is learned, not just inference compute. Tested only at tiny scale.

title: Transformers Efficiently Perform In-Context Logistic Regression via Normalized Gradient Descent
relevance_reason: Theory of looped softmax transformers as in-context learners: one trained layer, looped L times, implements L steps of normalized gradient descent.
one_sentence: Constructs L-layer softmax-attention transformers whose layers exactly perform L steps of normalized gradient descent on an in-context exponential loss, proves a single layer trained with a one-step GD teacher converges to this structure, and bounds OOD error of the looped model.
key_contributions: Theorem 4.1 (expressivity): attention-only L-layer softmax transformer outputs equal the first L NGD iterates on the in-context loss; Corollary 4.3: output converges in direction to the in-context max-margin (SVM) solution as L grows.
Theorem 4.5 (training): single softmax layer trained with one-step GD supervision has a unique minimizer and linear convergence to an NGD-implementing structure.
Theorem 4.7 (OOD): looping the trained layer L times gives a point-wise high-probability error bound O(log n/(alpha L) + d log rho / n) under log-concave test features.

setup.model_sizes: single softmax self-attention layer, input in R^{2d x (n+1)}; (n,d) in {(60,20),(100,25),(150,30)} in experiments
setup.train_tokens_or_data: synthetic in-context linear classification, Gaussian features, online batches of 400 context datasets
setup.loops_train: 1 layer trained (also end-to-end multi-layer looped training in experiments)
setup.loops_test: L loops of the trained layer
setup.benchmarks: in-context weight prediction

claims.claim: An L-layer softmax transformer can exactly implement L steps of normalized gradient descent on the in-context logistic (exponential) loss.
claims.evidence_quote: under appropriate parameterizations, the outputs of softmax attention layers exactly match the iterates of normalized gradient descent applied to the in-context loss

claims.claim: The construction is reachable by training one layer with a one-step GD teacher and then looping it; the looped model gets an OOD generalization guarantee.
claims.evidence_quote: we show that our constructed transformer can be obtained through (i) training a single self-attention layer supervised by one-step gradient descent, and (ii) recurrently applying the trained layer to obtain a looped model

claims.claim: Error of the looped model decays as O(log n / (alpha L)) in depth plus a statistical term, so more loops reduce the implicit-bias error.
claims.evidence_quote: Theorem 4.7 shows that its prediction error is controlled by the implicit-bias error from Corollary 4.3 and the finite-sample statistical error of the in-context maximum-margin solution.

limitations: Simplified in-context linear classification with exponential loss; attention-only construction; theory covers training one layer then looping, not end-to-end training of multi-layer looped models (observed empirically only).
survey_notes: Fits sub-theme (c) looped models as iterative optimizers / in-context learners. Extends the linear-regression GD story (2410.08292) to softmax attention and classification, and provides an OOD guarantee that improves with loop count, a theoretical counterpart of 'more loops = more optimizer steps'. No LM-scale test.

title: Fixed-Point RNNs: Interpolating from Diagonal to Dense
relevance_reason: Iterates a single diagonal linear-RNN layer in depth to a fixed point that realizes a dense RNN; depth-recurrent (implicit) sequence mixer rather than looped transformer LM.
one_sentence: Parameterizes dense linear RNNs implicitly as fixed points of parallelizable diagonal RNN iterations, so the number of fixed-point iterations trades parallelism for state-tracking expressivity at fixed parameters; a single FP-Mamba layer solves A5/S5 state tracking and copying.
key_contributions: Fixed-Point RNN framework: h = f_theta(x, h) solved by iterating a diagonal RNN; iteration count adaptively trades parallel computation for expressivity.
Stable parameterization of the implicit dense RNN; variants with Householder channel mixers and linear-attention-style matrix states (FP-Mamba).
Single-layer FP-Mamba-H solves A5 state tracking and copying where deeper Mamba/GatedDeltaNet baselines fail at one or the other; iterations adapt to task difficulty, fewer on language pretraining.

setup.model_sizes: single-layer FP-Mamba-H vs baselines of depth 1-8; up to ~100M params in Fig. 2 copying sweep
setup.train_tokens_or_data: A5/S5 state tracking (train length 16), copying (lengths 5-50), modular arithmetic; FineWeb language pretraining at context 2048
setup.loops_train: max fixed-point iterations l_max in {2,4,8,16}, or random Gamma(4,1)
setup.loops_test: iterate until convergence (l*)
setup.baselines: Mamba-1, Mamba-2, GatedDeltaNet, LSTM, Transformer
setup.benchmarks: A5, S5 state tracking, copying, modular arithmetic

claims.claim: Fixed-point iteration of a diagonal RNN lets a model trade parallelism for expressivity at a fixed number of parameters and reach state-of-the-art state-tracking accuracy.
claims.regime: iso_param (single layer, varying iterations) vs deeper baselines (unmatched depth)
claims.evidence_quote: The resulting models can naturally trade expressivity for efficiency at a fixed number of parameters and achieve state-of-the-art results on the state-tracking benchmarks A5 and S5 , while matching performance on copying and other tasks.

claims.claim: FP-RNNs adapt computation time to task difficulty by varying the number of fixed-point iterations; on simpler tasks the model effectively falls back to O(T) cost.
claims.evidence_quote: This suggests that the model adapts to O(T ) complexity on simpler tasks when the full state-tracking expressivity is not required.

claims.claim: The effective number of iterations adapts to difficulty: far fewer than sequence length on copying, modular arithmetic and language pretraining.
claims.evidence_quote: Fig. 7 shows that the model automatically adapts to using less fixed-point iterations on language pretraining at context length 2048.

limitations: Worst case FP-RNNs behave like nonlinear RNNs with O(T^2) runtime if iterations scale with sequence length; fixed-point convergence rate and kernel fusion left for future work; results mainly on toy tasks.
venue: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025).
survey_notes: Adjacent to 'expressivity': a component-level depth-recurrence (fixed-point iteration of one layer) that moves a model out of the TC0-like diagonal-SSM class toward RNN-like state tracking, with iterations as the expressivity knob. Empirical observation that needed iterations scale with sequence length for state tracking echoes the theoretical intuition that depth must grow with serial problem size (cf. 2502.17416 log-depth for group composition via a different mechanism). Cited by 2608.18222 as FPRM baseline.

title: On the Reasoning Abilities of Masked Diffusion Language Models
relevance_reason: Proves masked diffusion LMs are equivalent to padded looped transformers (finite precision, log width), giving circuit-class characterizations of PLTs by loop count and a CoT separation.
one_sentence: Shows finite-precision log-width masked diffusion models and polynomially padded looped transformers (PLTs) coincide up to log factors in padding, characterizes them as L-uniform AC0 (constant steps) and AC^d (log^d steps), and separates log-step MDM/PLT from log-step CoT.
key_contributions: Theorem 3.1: MDM[T,P] in PLT[T,P] and PLT[T,P] in MDM[T,(N+P)D]; Corollary 3.1: MDM[T, O~(N^K)] = PLT[T, O(N^K)].
Via PLT results: MDM/PLT with O(1) steps and poly padding = L-uniform AC0; with O(log^d N) steps = L-uniform AC^d; regular languages in MDM[log N, N].
MDMs and CoT simulate each other with polynomial overheads (MDM with poly steps stays in P); strict separation CoT[log N] subsetneq MDM[log N, N] assuming TC0 != NC1.

claims.claim: In the finite-precision log-width setting, masked diffusion models and polynomially padded looped transformers are equivalent, and MDMs can solve everything CoT transformers can.
claims.evidence_quote: We show that MDMs and polynomially-padded PLTs are, in fact, equivalent in this setting, and that MDMs can solve all problems that CoT-augmented transformers can.

claims.claim: Padded looped transformers (and MDMs) with constantly many steps and polynomial padding equal L-uniform AC0; more loops (log^d N) raise expressivity to L-uniform AC^d, approaching NC with polylog loops.
claims.evidence_quote: we get that with polylogarithmic looping and polynomial padding, MDMs converge to NC, the class of all parallelizable problems

claims.claim: With logarithmically many steps, CoT transformers stay in TC0 while MDMs (hence PLTs with linear padding) recognize all regular languages including NC1-complete ones, a strict separation under TC0 != NC1.
claims.evidence_quote: While CoT transformers remain in TC0 , MDMs can solve NC1 -complete problems.

limitations: Idealized MDM with planner and predictor and resampling; finite-precision log-width setting; existence results only, no learnability or experiments; simulations incur polynomial padding blow-ups.
venue: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026
survey_notes: Gives the cleanest circuit-class ladder for padded looped transformers indexed by loop count (O(1) -> AC0, log^d N -> AC^d) in finite precision, the counterpart of Merrill & Sabharwal's log-precision TC^d results. Its CoT separation (looping wins with few steps on parallelizable problems) is the opposite direction from 2605.30757 (CoT wins with polynomial steps against compressed-state loops); they are consistent because PLTs carry per-position state plus padding (memory-rich) and the step budgets differ. Agrees with 2509.25239 (latent thought advantage on parallelizable problems). Not tested empirically.

title: Unlocking Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Transformers via Recursive Latent Space Reasoning
relevance_reason: Input-adaptive recurrent-depth transformer with per-iteration algorithmic supervision, discrete latent anchoring and error correction for OOD algorithmic generalization.
one_sentence: On GSM8K-style modular arithmetic over computational graphs, a recurrent transformer with input-adaptive depth, step-wise algorithmic supervision, discretize-and-re-embed latents and trained error correction generalizes near-perfectly from graphs with up to 32 nodes to 128 nodes, where CoT degrades.
key_contributions: Four mechanisms: input-adaptive recurrence, algorithmic (per-step) supervision, anchored discrete latent bottleneck between iterations, explicit error correction via latent corruption during training.

Ablations: continuous latent supervision beats CoT but degrades with depth (noise accumulation); discretization anchors latents; error correction gives near-perfect OOD but needs more layers per block.
Mechanistic interpretability analysis of the learned depth-invariant recursive circuits.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: synthetic modular arithmetic on computational graphs with N <= 32 nodes
setup.loops_train: number of recurrent iterations tied to graph depth (algorithmic supervision per step)
setup.loops_test: scaled with problem size; graphs up to N = 128
setup.baselines: End-to-End transformer, Chain-of-Thought trained transformer, continuous latent supervision
setup.benchmarks: % fully solved on graphs of 8-128 nodes

claims.claim: CoT-trained transformers generalize only modestly beyond training size (to about 40 nodes from <= 32) and degrade rapidly.
claims.evidence_quote: While the best-performing CoT models exhibit a limited degree of OOD generalization to moderately larger graphs (N ≤ 32 ; N ≈ 40), this capability rapidly deteriorates as graph sizes exceed the training regime.

claims.claim: With all four mechanisms, the recurrent model achieves near-perfect performance on all OOD splits, i.e. on graphs several times larger than training.
claims.evidence_quote: When all proposed ingredients are incorporated, i.e., Discrete Latent Space Supervision ⟲1 , the model robustly achieves near-perfect performance across all OOD splits we examined.

claims.claim: Continuous latent recurrence degrades with more recurrent depth because noise accumulates and representations drift; discretizing and re-embedding between iterations anchors states and fixes this.
claims.evidence_quote: We attribute this to accumulating noise in the continuous vector representations — a phenomenon exacerbated when scaling test-time compute for larger problem instances — which eventually causes representations to drift

numbers.value: train N <= 32, test up to N = 128 (fourfold)
numbers.quote: training Transformer models on problem instances with N ≤ 32 nodes and testing them on instances of varying sizes, up to N = 128 (a fourfold increase).

limitations: Single synthetic task family; requires step-wise algorithmic supervision (reference algorithm traces); hyperparameter sensitivity noted; extension to less structured, multi-task settings left open.
survey_notes: Length/size generalization sub-theme: adds discretization between loops (anchoring) and error-correction training as ingredients beyond input injection and adaptive steps. Its continuous-latent degradation is the same 'drift with depth' failure analyzed in 2608.18222 and overthinking in 2202.05826. Requires intermediate supervision, unlike 2409.15647 (only final answer + step count). Untested at LM scale.

title: Enhancing Auto-regressive Chain-of-Thought through Loop-Aligned Reasoning
relevance_reason: Aligns looped-transformer iterations with CoT steps; uses the looped model's length generalization to generate CoT data for an autoregressive model.
one_sentence: Trains an encoder-only looped transformer whose iteration count equals problem complexity, with per-iteration supervision aligned to CoT steps, then uses its length-generalizing CoT outputs to fine-tune an autoregressive CoT model on longer problems.
key_contributions: Shows a single looped transformer (3 layers, 256-dim) jointly trained on Arithmetic, Edit Distance and LIS length-generalizes better than an autoregressive CoT transformer of the same configuration.
Iteration-wise alignment: loop t is supervised to emit the CoT tokens of reasoning round t, preserving length generalization and making intermediate steps explicit.
RELAY: looped-model-generated CoT chains for longer problems are used to fine-tune the autoregressive model, which then improves beyond its training length.

setup.model_sizes: 3 layers, 256-dimensional hidden states, 4 heads for all models; RoPE
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 1M training / 100k test samples per task; train lengths <= 15 (Arithmetic), <= 30 (ED), <= 100 (LIS)
setup.loops_train: number of loop iterations set equal to problem complexity
setup.loops_test: same rule on longer problems: [15,25], [30,40], [100,120]
setup.baselines: autoregressive CoT decoder transformer with same configuration; vanilla looped model without CoT alignment
setup.benchmarks: Arithmetic, Edit Distance, Longest Increasing Subsequence

claims.claim: Within training lengths both models are perfect, but beyond them the autoregressive CoT model deteriorates while the looped transformer stays better at all lengths.
claims.evidence_quote: While the auto-regressive CoT Transformer’s performance deteriorates significantly, the looped Transformer maintains superior performance across all length regimes.

claims.claim: Supervising each loop iteration with the corresponding CoT step preserves and even improves the looped model's length generalization.
claims.evidence_quote: This additional iteration-wise supervision not only preserves the Looped Transformer’s ability for length generalization but also enables it to predict CoT reasoning steps for unseen data.

claims.claim: Fine-tuning the autoregressive model on looped-model-generated long CoT chains significantly improves it beyond the original training length, approaching the looped model.
claims.evidence_quote: the auto-regressive CoT model fine-tuned with data generated by RELAY (i.e., by the looped model with explicit CoT alignment) exhibits significant improvements on problems exceeding the original training length

numbers.quote: The architectural configuration remains consistent across all models, comprising 3 layers, 256-dimensional hidden states, and 4 attention heads.

limitations: Loop count must be set to problem complexity (hard for general tasks like translation); synthetic tasks only; small models; work in progress, no theory of why looped models length-generalize.
survey_notes: Empirical counterpart to the looped-vs-CoT theory: at equal (tiny) parameters, looped models extrapolate where CoT fails, and looped models can be used as teachers for CoT. Loop count is tied to problem complexity, the same coupling 2606.29983 identifies as a source of OOD variance. Comparison is iso-param but not iso-compute (CoT generates many more tokens; looped uses T passes). Not LM scale.

title: A Formal Comparison Between Chain of Thought and Latent Thought
relevance_reason: Two-way formal separation between looped/latent-thought reasoning and CoT: looping wins on parallel computation, CoT wins on approximate counting/sampling.
one_sentence: Proves looped transformers (and Coconut) with log^k n iterations and polynomial padding exactly capture AC^k/TC^k, while CoT with log^k n steps stays in TC^{k-1}, giving strict separations for latent thought; conversely CoT's stochastic decoding admits approximate counting/sampling that deterministic latent thought cannot.
key_contributions: Theorem 3.12: Loop[log^k n, poly(n), 1 (resp. log n)] = CT[...] = AC^k (resp. TC^k); Lemma 3.13: CoT[log^k n, poly(n), log n] in TC^{k-1}; Theorems 3.14-3.15: strict separations under TC^{k-1} != NC^k / TC^k.
Theorem 3.10: circuit depth maps to loop iterations (DEPTH[T] in Loop[T, size, 1]) while CoT steps map to circuit size (Li et al.).

Lemma 4.3/Theorems 4.4-4.5: assuming FPTAS != FPRAS for self-reducible relations, polynomial CoT admits FPRAS/approximate sampling that polynomial-iteration latent thought cannot; pLoop[poly] and pCT[poly] are strictly contained in pCoT[poly].

setup.train_tokens_or_data: synthetic tasks: word problems for non-solvable groups, s-t connectivity, arithmetic expression evaluation, edit distance; DNF counting, graph coloring sampling
setup.loops_train: varied (2 to 64 iterations depending on task)
setup.loops_test: same
setup.baselines: CoT with full or reduced steps (uniform step selection or stepwise internalization)
setup.benchmarks: accuracy on parallelizable tasks; relative counting error; TV distance to uniform over colorings

claims.claim: Latent thought with log^k n iterations exactly captures TC^k (log precision) / AC^k, while CoT with log^k n steps is upper-bounded by TC^{k-1}, so latent thought is strictly more efficient on parallelizable problems under standard assumptions.
claims.evidence_quote: We show that latent thought with logk n iterations exactly captures the power of TCk (Thm. 3.12); in contrast, CoT with logk n steps cannot realize the full power of TCk (Thm. 3.13) due to its inherent sequentiality.

claims.claim: CoT with stochastic decoding admits approximate counting (FPRAS) and approximate uniform sampling that deterministic latent thought with polynomially many iterations cannot, the first formal separation in favor of CoT.
claims.evidence_quote: there exist target distributions that CoT can approximately represent and sample from, but that remain inaccessible to latent thought (Theorem 4.4). To the best of our knowledge, this constitutes the first formal separation in favor of CoT.

claims.claim: Empirically, looped transformers solve parallelizable tasks with fewer iterations than CoT needs, and the loops needed grow only logarithmically with input size.
claims.regime: not_applicable (small synthetic models; iteration counts compared, not compute)
claims.evidence_quote: as the input size n increases, the number of loops required to maintain high accuracy grows only logarithmically, supporting our theoretical claim in the (poly-)logarithmic regime

claims.claim: On graph-coloring sampling, CoT covers valid colorings more uniformly than the looped model, which concentrates mass on fewer solutions.
claims.evidence_quote: uniform, whereas the looped model concentrates probability mass on a smaller subset of solutions. This indicates that CoT achieves more uniform coverage of the valid colorings.

limitations: Expressivity results with padded looped models; separations conditional on unproven complexity assumptions; small synthetic experiments; extension to realistic downstream tasks left open.
venue: Proceedings of the 43 rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea. PMLR 306, 2026.
survey_notes: Central to sub-theme (b): refines 2502.17416 Thm 5.4 (looped >= deterministic CoT) by showing it fails for stochastic CoT. Loop iterations ~ circuit depth, CoT steps ~ circuit size: a clean statement of why recurrent depth is a different scaling axis from generated tokens. Must be read with 2605.30757: the looped model here is a padded sequence-state loop (memory-rich), so the CoT-favoring separations come from stochasticity here and from memory there. Agrees with 2510.13117 (MDM/PLT vs CoT at log steps). Not tested at LM scale.

title: On Expressive Power of Looped Transformers: Theoretical Analysis and Enhancement via Timestep Encoding
relevance_reason: First approximation-rate (universality) theory for looped transformers; motivates timestep-conditioned scaling per loop.
one_sentence: Derives the approximation rate of single-layer looped transformers for continuous permutation-equivariant seq2seq functions in terms of loop count and three moduli of continuity, identifies a looping-specific error term, and adds timestep-conditioned scaling (TMLT) that improves reasoning, ICL and WikiText-103 results.
key_contributions: Theorem 3.6: approximation error of L2 o TF^{o r} o L1 bounded by sequence, contextual and token moduli of continuity at scale delta = ((r-N)/2)^{-1/((N+1)d+1)} plus terms in parameter magnitude; more loops reduce error. Corollary 3.7: universality (density in permutation-equivariant continuous functions).
Identifies extra moduli (contextual and token continuity) as an intrinsic limitation of weight tying; Theorem 4.2: time-dependent scaling parameters remove it.
Timestep encoding (frequency embedding + MLP) to modulate each loop; experiments on Sudoku, Countdown, LCS, edit distance, in-context decision trees and WikiText-103.

setup.model_sizes: single-layer looped TF vs standard TF with L=6 or 12 layers
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Sudoku 3M train; Countdown 5M; ED/LCS 10^6 train; WikiText-103 (>100M tokens)
setup.loops_train: r from 4 up to 100 depending on task; r=12 (ICL), r=24 (WikiText-103)
setup.loops_test: same as training
setup.baselines: standard Transformer (L=6, L=12), looped TF without timestep encoding
setup.benchmarks: Sudoku, Countdown, LCS, edit distance, in-context decision trees (MSE), WikiText-103 perplexity

claims.claim: Theorem 3.6 / Corollary 3.7: single-layer looped transformers with fixed width (two heads, head size 1, width O(d)) universally approximate continuous permutation-equivariant seq2seq functions, with error decreasing as loop count r grows (under infinite-precision weights).
claims.evidence_quote: Theorem 3.6 shows that increasing the number of loops r reduces the approximation error. Under infinite-precision weights, this leads to a universal approximation theorem.

claims.claim: The rate contains two additional moduli of continuity beyond the ReLU-network case, an error amplification intrinsic to weight tying; timestep-dependent scaling per loop removes it.
claims.evidence_quote: The approximation rate in Theorem 3.6 includes two additional moduli of continuity, which can lead to increased errors, reflecting a limitation inherent to Looped Transformers.

claims.claim: Empirically, more loops improve reasoning-task accuracy, higher loop counts significantly outperform standard transformers, and timestep encoding adds further gains.
claims.regime: unmatched (looped single layer vs 6/12-layer TF; neither iso-param nor iso-FLOP stated precisely)
claims.evidence_quote: The results in Table 2 demonstrate that increasing the number of loops improves performance on reasoning tasks, with higher loop counts significantly outperforming standard Transformers.

numbers.value: TF L=12: 8.6e-03; Looped r=12: 1.4e-02; with timestep r=12: 1.7e-03
numbers.quote: TF L=12 8.6e-03 Looped r=12 1.4e-02 w/ Timestep r=12 1.7e-03

Provides a theoretical rationale for step/timestep conditioning in loops, a design choice that contrasts with Huginn's finding that step-conditioning hurts path independence/extrapolation (landmarks 2502.05171). Flag as a tension: timestep encodings help fixed-r approximation but may break extrapolation to unseen r. Statistical counterpart: 2609.25778. WikiText-103 is the only LM-scale-ish test (small).

title: Looped ReLU MLPs May Be All You Need as Practical Programmable Computers
relevance_reason: Constructive universality result for a looped (weight-tied) 23-layer ReLU-MLP, extending 2301.13196 beyond attention.
one_sentence: Proves a looped 23-layer ReLU-MLP of width n (state vector holding memory, scratchpad, instructions) emulates SUBLEQ and hence a programmable (Turing-complete given memory) computer, with O(n log n) per-pass cost via low-rank factorization versus O(n^2) for the looped transformer of 2301.13196.
key_contributions: Theorem 4.1/E.1: a 23-layer ReLU-MLP of width n, looped, emulates d-bit SUBLEQ, i.e. a one-instruction-set computer.
MLP gadgets for read, write, addition, subtraction and conditional branching.
Low-rank decomposition gives O(n log n) parameters and per-pass time, contrasted with O(n^2) attention in looped transformers.

setup.model_sizes: 23-layer ReLU-MLP with width n
setup.loops_test: one loop per SUBLEQ instruction
setup.baselines: 2301.13196 looped transformer (comparison of per-pass complexity)

claims.claim: A looped 23-layer ReLU-MLP with width n can emulate a programmable computer (SUBLEQ OISC), so attention is not necessary for looped universality.
claims.evidence_quote: we provide an aﬃrmative answer that a looped 23-layer ReLU-MLP is capable of performing the basic necessary operations, more eﬃciently and eﬀectively functioning as a programmable computer than a looped Transformer

claims.claim: With low-rank decomposition each forward pass costs O(n log n) versus O(n^2) for the looped transformer construction.
claims.evidence_quote: each forward pass of our 23-layer ReLU-MLP only takes O(n log n) time complexity, while looped Transformer in [GRS+ 23] takes O(n2 ) time complexity for each forward pass
