survey_notes: Expressivity sub-theme: universality of looping is architecture-agnostic (holds for MLPs), so it says little about why looped transformers in particular help; weakens arguments that use Turing-completeness constructions to motivate looped LMs. Abstract says 'looped 9-layer Transformer' consistent with 2301.13196 Lemma 4 (whereas 2604.08816 says 10 layers).

title: Can Looped Transformers Learn to Implement Multi-step Gradient Descent for In-context Learning?
relevance_reason: First learnability (landscape + gradient-flow convergence) result for a multi-layer, weight-tied (looped) linear transformer on in-context regression.
one_sentence: For in-context linear regression with Gaussian data, proves the global minimizer of a linear looped transformer implements L steps of preconditioned GD with preconditioner near the inverse population covariance, and that gradient flow converges despite non-convexity via a new gradient-dominance condition.
key_contributions: Theorem 3.2: global minimizers of the population loss have u_opt = 0 and (1-c) Sigma*^{-1} <= A_opt <= (1+c) Sigma*^{-1}, i.e. exactly L steps of preconditioned GD.
Theorem 3.3-3.4: gradient flow converges to the vicinity of the optimum, via a gradient-dominance inequality with power (2L-1)/L.
Experiments: 1-layer model looped L times performs like an L-layer non-looped model; models trained with 2 or 5 loops keep improving when run with more loops at test time, ID and OOD.

setup.model_sizes: linear self-attention looped model, dimension d = 5 in experiments
setup.train_tokens_or_data: in-context linear regression, Gaussian inputs with identity covariance
setup.loops_train: L loops (e.g. 2, 5 and more)
setup.loops_test: arbitrarily many loops at test time
setup.baselines: multi-layer non-looped linear transformers
setup.benchmarks: in-context regression loss ID and OOD (different covariance)

claims.claim: The global minimizer of the population loss for a linear looped transformer with L loops implements L steps of preconditioned gradient descent with a data-adapted preconditioner.
claims.evidence_quote: we show that the global minimizer of the population training loss implements multi-step preconditioned gradient descent, with a preconditioner that adapts to the data distribution

claims.claim: Gradient flow converges fast despite non-convexity, the first such convergence result beyond one-layer transformers in this setting.
claims.evidence_quote: we show a fast convergence for gradient flow on the regression loss, despite the non-convexity of the landscape, by proving a novel gradient dominance condition

claims.claim: Empirically, a 1-layer model looped L times performs similarly to an L-layer model, and models trained with few loops keep improving when looped more at test time, ID and OOD.
claims.evidence_quote: For looped models trained with just few loops (2, or 5), evaluating with more loops keeps improving the loss in both cases, suggesting that it learned the correct iterative algorithm.

limitations: Linear attention, Gaussian in-context linear regression only; theory needs many in-context samples relative to dimension; non-looped multi-layer convergence and nonlinear attention left open; test-time improvement beyond trained loops observed but not proved.
survey_notes: Sub-theme (c): looped models as optimizers. Provides learnability (not just expressivity) for weight-tied depth, and a mechanistic reason test-time loop extrapolation can work: the learned map is a convergent fixed-point iteration (cf. 2608.18222 settling operators, 2202.05826). Same authors as 2502.17416. Saunshi et al. cite it as ICML 2024 but the text here carries no venue line.

title: On Logical Extrapolation for Mazes with Recurrent and Implicit Networks
relevance_reason: Probes whether weight-tied recurrent (DT-Net) and implicit (DEQ) networks that extrapolate by iterating longer actually learned algorithms; convergence analysis of the iteration.
one_sentence: Stress-tests pretrained maze extrapolators (DT-Net RNN of 2202.05826, INN/DEQ of Anil et al.) along new difficulty axes (cycles, non-deadend starts), finds partial algorithm learning (approximate deadend-filling) and goal misgeneralization, and shows extrapolators can succeed while converging to limit cycles rather than fixed points.
key_contributions: New distribution shifts (percolation/cycles, deadend start) reveal failures of models that extrapolate in maze size.
Evidence DT-Net approximately learned deadend-filling (agrees on 98.8% of 143k test mazes) but fails where deadend-filling would succeed.

TDA analysis of latent trajectories: INN converges to fixed points; DT-Net RNN can converge to limit cycles yet still be correct; more diverse training data helps accuracy but reduces size extrapolation.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: maze-dataset; pretrained models from Bansal et al. 2022 and Anil et al. 2022; retrained with percolation p > 0
setup.loops_test: increased iterations for larger mazes
setup.baselines: DT-Net (2202.05826) and PI-INN (Anil et al. 2022)
setup.benchmarks: maze solving under size, percolation and deadend-start shifts

claims.claim: Models that extrapolate in maze size fail in various ways under other difficulty shifts; whether they learned an algorithm remains uncertain.
claims.evidence_quote: By varying test data along multiple axes — not just maze size — we show that models introduced in prior work fail in a variety of ways, some expected and others less so.

claims.claim: Training on more diverse data (mazes with cycles) improves accuracy on cycles but paradoxically does not improve logical extrapolation.
claims.evidence_quote: We show that training these models on more diverse data addresses some failure modes but, paradoxically, does not improve logical extrapolation.

claims.claim: Logical extrapolators can succeed without fixed-point convergence: the DT-Net RNN sometimes enters limit cycles yet is as performant, complicating the fixed-point view of 2202.05826.
claims.evidence_quote: we show that logical extrapolators can succeed even when their iterative part does not converge to a fixed point, and identify and quantify two exotic limiting behaviors

numbers.quote: the output of the RNN agrees with deadend-filling on 98.8% of 143k tests mazes across a variety of sizes and percolation values

limitations: Single task (maze solving); philosophical ambiguity about what 'learning an algorithm' means and which shifts are reasonable.
survey_notes: Important caution for the length/size-generalization sub-theme: extrapolation along the trained difficulty axis does not imply the learned procedure is the intended algorithm (goal misgeneralization). Partly contradicts 2202.05826's fixed-point account (limit cycles also succeed) and nuances 2608.18222 (which ties useful depth to settling; here non-settling limit cycles can still be correct in answer space, consistent with 2608.18222's weak-form R4). Not language.

title: Unveiling Transformers with LEGO: a synthetic reasoning task
relevance_reason: Synthetic chain-of-reasoning task where weight-tied ALBERT (looped) length-extrapolates better than BERT; stochastic-depth training of the tied model further helps. Looping is one of several factors studied.
one_sentence: Introduces LEGO (resolving chains of variable assignments under group operations) and finds weight-tied ALBERT extrapolates to longer chains where BERT does not, behaves more like a for-loop in probing, and extrapolates further when trained with stochastic depth.
key_contributions: LEGO task for studying chain-following and length extrapolation (train supervision on first 6 variables, test on 12).
Iterative (weight-shared) ALBERT extrapolates beyond supervised variables while BERT does not; probing shows ALBERT's information percolation is closer to linear in depth (a for-loop bias).
Stochastic depth for ALBERT (depth sampled 6-12 in training, 12 at test) improves length extrapolation; pretraining helps via structured attention heads; LEGO attention module reduces FLOPs.

setup.model_sizes: BERT and ALBERT (12 layers), random init or pretrained
setup.train_tokens_or_data: synthetic LEGO sequences, n = 12 variables, supervision on n_tr = 6 or 12
setup.loops_train: 12 tied layers; stochastic depth variant samples 6-12
setup.baselines: BERT (untied), pretrained BERT
setup.benchmarks: per-variable accuracy on LEGO

claims.claim: Weight-tied ALBERT extrapolates to longer reasoning chains than untied BERT of the same depth: near-perfect on two unsupervised variables and nontrivial on a third, vs barely above random for BERT on one.
claims.regime: iso_effective_depth (12 tied vs 12 untied layers), iso_data
claims.evidence_quote: the iterative ALBERT reaches near-perfect accuracy on two additional variables (#6 and #7), and nontrivial accuracy on the third (#8). These results clearly support that iterative architectures do generalize better in the iterative LEGO reasoning task.

claims.claim: Training ALBERT with stochastic depth (randomized loop count) further improves length extrapolation.
claims.evidence_quote: We uniformly sample depth between 6 and 12 per batch during training while fixing it at 12 during test. Figure 5 shows a clear improvement in generalization to longer lengths using stochastic depth.

limitations: Single synthetic task; looping studied only as ALBERT-style full weight sharing at fixed depth; extrapolation gains are a few extra chain steps.
survey_notes: Early evidence (2022) for the inductive bias later formalized in 2502.17416: tied depth behaves like a for-loop and extrapolates on chain-following. Randomized depth during training as stabilizer anticipates 2202.05826 progressive loss, 2606.29983 stochastic loop counts and Huginn randomized recurrence. Iso-effective-depth comparison but extrapolation is only a few steps.

title: The Devil is in the Detail: Simple Tricks Improve Systematic Generalization of Transformers
relevance_reason: Compares standard vs Universal (weight-shared) Transformers on systematic/length generalization; weight sharing is one of several tricks studied.
one_sentence: Shows baseline Transformers on SCAN, CFQ, PCFG, COGS and Mathematics are badly under-tuned: embedding scaling, early stopping, relative positional embeddings and Universal (weight-shared, no ACT, no timestep embedding) variants drastically improve systematic generalization.
key_contributions: Configuration tricks (embedding scaling, early stopping on generalization split, relative PE) raise PCFG productivity from 50% to 85% and COGS from 35% to 81%.
Universal Transformer variants (shared layers, no ACT, no timestep embedding) outperform standard Transformers on most datasets except COGS and CFQ MCD 1.
Shows IID validation hides these differences; calls for generalization validation splits.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: SCAN, CFQ, PCFG, COGS, Mathematics dataset
setup.loops_train: fixed number of shared layers
setup.loops_test: same
setup.baselines: standard Transformers with absolute/relative PE; published dataset baselines
setup.benchmarks: SCAN length split, CFQ (output length, MCD), PCFG (productivity/systematicity), COGS, Mathematics

claims.claim: Universal (weight-shared) Transformer variants outperform standard Transformers on most systematic generalization datasets, except COGS and CFQ MCD 1.
claims.regime: iso_effective_depth (same layer count, shared vs unshared; hyperparameters per dataset)
claims.evidence_quote: Except for COGS and CFQ MCD 1, the universal variants outperform the standard ones.

claims.claim: On the CFQ output-length split, the Universal Transformer without timestep embedding beats the previously reported UT (77% vs about 66%), and with relative PE reaches 81%.
claims.evidence_quote: The only architectural difference between the models is that ours does not make use of any timestep (i.e. layer ID) embedding.

numbers.what: CFQ output length split, UT absolute PE vs reported
numbers.quote: On the output length split of CFQ, our Universal Transformer with absolute positional embedding achieves significantly better performance than the one reported in Keysers et al. (2020): 77% versus ∼ 66%
Our models improve accuracy from 50% to 85% on the PCFG productivity split, and from 35% to 81% on COGS.

limitations: Improvements come from several tricks jointly; weight sharing not isolated at matched parameters; UT capacity limited by sharing.
survey_notes: Early systematic-generalization evidence for weight-shared depth; notes that dropping timestep (layer-ID) embedding coincided with a large CFQ length-split gain, which aligns with Huginn's observation that step conditioning hurts extrapolation and is in tension with 2410.01405's timestep-encoding gains (fixed-r approximation). Mixed results (UT loses on COGS, CFQ MCD1).

title: On the Mirage of Long-Range Dependency, with an Application to Integer Multiplication
relevance_reason: Iterated weight-shared local update (neural cellular automaton) for length generalization; iterated transformer variants fail. Not a looped LM.
one_sentence: Argues multiplication's long-range dependency is an artifact of the 1D representation: on a 2D outer-product grid a 321-parameter neural cellular automaton, iterated about n+2 steps, multiplies perfectly up to 683x the training length, while iterated Transformer and Mamba updates fail.
key_contributions: Formal notion of 'mirage' dependency induced by the computational spacetime (representation plus architecture time depth).
2D outer-product layout makes each long-multiplication step a 3x3 local operation; NCA learns it with single-step training and iterates stably.
Transformer (6,625 params), Transformer+RoPE, Mamba and MLP all fit the single-step target but fail under multi-step iteration.

setup.model_sizes: NCA 321 parameters; Transformer 6,625; Mamba 4,577
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 2- to 6-bit integer pairs
setup.loops_train: single-step targets (Chaos Training)
setup.loops_test: iterate until done, about n+2 steps, up to 4,096 bits
setup.baselines: Transformer (sinusoidal, RoPE), Mamba, MLP with the same encoding
setup.benchmarks: binary integer multiplication exact match

claims.claim: A 321-parameter NCA iterated on a 2D grid achieves 100% accuracy from 16 to 4,096 bits after training on 2-6 bits, with steps scaling linearly in n.
claims.evidence_quote: The model achieves 100% accuracy within the training range (2–6 bits) and maintains 100% on all tested out-of-distribution lengths — from 16 bits up to 4,096 bits (2,467 decimal digits), achieving 683 × length generalization.

claims.claim: Iterated transformers fail not because they cannot fit one step but because softmax attention distributions are size-dependent and the update cannot be iterated stably on larger grids.
claims.evidence_quote: The problem is not that these architectures cannot fit the single-step target, but that they cannot stably iterate the learned update.

limitations: Single task; relies on a hand-designed 2D representation; single-author preprint.
survey_notes: Peripheral for length generalization: shows the representation/locality, not iteration per se, decides extrapolation; iterating a transformer update is unstable across sizes (consistent with 2608.31067's finding that plain looped transformers collapse OOD without structured masking).

title: Bifurcation Models: Learning Set-Valued Solution Maps with Weight-Tied Dynamics
relevance_reason: Theory of weight-tied iterated dynamics (equilibrium models) representing multi-solution maps via multiple attractors; scientific tasks, not LMs.
one_sentence: Shows weight-tied dynamics y_{t+1} = g(y_t, x) can represent set-valued solution maps as multiple stable equilibria reached from different initializations, with almost-everywhere regular induced selectors, unlike arbitrary single-branch labels; validated on frustrated Ising and Allen-Cahn problems.
key_contributions: Representation theorem: set-valued maps with locally Lipschitz branches are realized by regular equilibrium dynamics (Theorem 2.2).
Induced selectors of the dynamics are almost everywhere regular (Theorem 2.3), whereas manual selectors can be arbitrarily irregular (Theorem 2.4).
Experiments: dynamics discover multiple valid equilibria without branch labels on frustrated Ising models; diversity must be encouraged explicitly on Allen-Cahn (accuracy-diversity tradeoff).

setup.train_tokens_or_data: frustrated Ising models, Allen-Cahn equation
setup.loops_test: iterate to equilibrium from different initializations
setup.baselines: single-branch supervised fitting

claims.claim: Broad set-valued maps with locally Lipschitz branches can be represented by regular weight-tied equilibrium dynamics whose induced selectors are almost everywhere regular, while manually chosen single-branch selectors can be arbitrarily irregular.
claims.evidence_quote: We prove that broad set-valued maps with locally Lipschitz branches can be represented by regular equilibrium dynamics and that the induced selectors are almost everywhere regular, while manual selectors can be arbitrarily irregular.

limitations: Scientific toy problems; diversity of discovered equilibria not automatic.
survey_notes: Peripheral; relevant to the fixed-point/attractor view of looped models (2608.18222) and to multi-solution tasks like Sudoku where DART (2609.05988) and 2608.18222 note multiple valid completions. Different initial states -> different attractors suggests random-init latent states (as in Huginn) can encode solution multiplicity.

title: Advancing the Understanding of Fixed Point Iterations in Deep Neural Networks: A Detailed Analytical Study
relevance_reason: Analytical conditions for (multiple, robust) fixed points of looped neural networks; small-scale theory with preliminary experiments.
one_sentence: Gives a sufficient condition for the existence of multiple fixed points of looped neural networks across input regions, extends it to robust fixed points, and shows looped networks with exponential or polynomial activations can have 2^d robust fixed points.
key_contributions: Sufficient condition for multiple fixed points of looped (iterated) vector-valued neural networks based on input regions.
Robust fixed-point iteration analysis; case studies with 2^d robust fixed points for exponentiation/polynomial activations.
Preliminary empirical support.

claims.claim: Looped neural networks can have exponentially many (2^d) robust fixed points under exponential or polynomial activations, via a sufficient condition based on input regions.
claims.evidence_quote: we provide case studies that looped neural networks may exist 2d number of robust fixed points under exponentiation or polynomial activation functions, where d is the feature dimension

limitations: Analysis of simple vector-valued looped networks, not transformers or LMs; preliminary experiments only.
survey_notes: Peripheral theory supporting the fixed-point view of looping (2202.05826, 2608.18222, 2605.07277); motivated by empirical observation that hidden states stabilize after several layers (basis for early exit and layer looping).

title: AlgoFormer: An Efficient Transformer Framework with Algorithmic Structures
relevance_reason: Pre-transformer + looped transformer + post-transformer (sandwich) design with expressivity theorems for iterative algorithms; assignment title 'On the Expressive Power of a Variant of the Looped Transformer' is this paper's earlier title (arXiv 2402.13572 as cited by 2502.17416).
one_sentence: Proposes AlgoFormer (pre-transformer for preprocessing, looped transformer for iterative optimization, post-transformer for readout), proves constructions for regression/CoT-like tasks and Newton's method, and reports gains over standard and vanilla looped transformers on synthetic tasks and small NMT/classification.
key_contributions: Sandwich architecture mirroring human-designed algorithms: TF_pre, looped TF_loop, TF_post.
Expressivity theorems: e.g. Theorem 4.1, one-layer two-head pre, loop and two-layer post transformers implement Newton's method for regression with arbitrarily small per-step error.
Training with loss averaged over loop iterations T0..T (window Delta T) to encourage generalization beyond training loops; small NMT (IWSLT De-En) and text classification experiments.

setup.loops_test: also longer loop counts in synthetic tasks

setup.benchmarks: regression/ICL MSE, BLEU and cross-entropy on IWSLT De-En, classification accuracy

claims.evidence_quote: However, the error can be made arbitrarily close to zero by increasing the temperature of the softmax and adjusting another free parameter, neither of which affects the size of the network.

claims.evidence_quote: As shown in the results, AlgoFormer outperforms and performs comparably with the standard Transformer and the vanilla looped Transformer in the Neural Machine Translation and Text Classification tasks

title: Reasoning with Latent Thoughts: On the Power of Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Foundational theory + 1B-scale empirical study of whole-stack weight-tied looping for reasoning, with looped-simulates-CoT theorem.
one_sentence: Shows k-layer blocks looped L times nearly match kL-layer models on synthetic reasoning and, at 1B LM scale, on reasoning benchmarks despite worse perplexity; proves log-depth looped constructions for group composition and p-hop, and that m loops simulate m CoT steps.
key_contributions: Empirical: (k⊗L) looped models match iso-depth (kL⊗1) baselines on addition, p-hop, i-GSM; at LM scale they recover a larger % of the gap on reasoning tasks than on perplexity/closed-book QA.

Theory: 1-layer looped transformer solves n-element group composition in ceil(log2 n) loops; any L-layer transformer with R distinct layers is simulated by a looped 1-layer block; p-hop in floor(log2 p)+2 loops; L+O(1)-layer looped model simulates m CoT steps with m loops on m padding tokens.
Looping-inspired cosine-similarity regularizer between layer blocks improves reasoning at neutral perplexity.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: 250B tokens of the Pile; all models see exactly the same tokens in the same order
setup.loops_train: fixed L (e.g. 24/k for LM; 12/k for addition; up to 12 for scaling study (4⊗L), L in {1,2,3,6,9,12})
setup.loops_test: same as training
setup.baselines: iso-param (k⊗1) and iso-FLOP/iso-depth (kL⊗1) non-looped transformers; middle-looping variant

claims.claim: On synthetic reasoning tasks, a k-layer block looped L times nearly matches a kL-layer non-looped model and far outperforms the k-layer model.
claims.evidence_quote: a k-layer transformer looped L times nearly matches the performance of a kL-layer non-looped model, and is significantly better than a k-layer model

claims.claim: At LM scale, looped models have worse perplexity than the iso-depth baseline but recover far more of the gap on reasoning-heavy downstream groups (open-book QA, math word problems, reasoning primitives) than on memorization (closed-book QA).
claims.evidence_quote: Overall the looped models are worse on perplexity and closed book QA (memorization benchmarks), but the % Gap is much higher for task groups that require reasoning (open book QA, math word problems).

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1: for any finite group, a constant-precision 1-layer transformer looped ceil(log2 n) times computes composition of n elements, matching the best known non-looped depth.
claims.evidence_quote: there exists a constant-precision looped transformer TFθ,T computing the composition of n elements from G with a 1-layer transformer block, T = ⌈log2 n⌉ loops

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2: any L-layer transformer with at most R distinct layers is simulated exactly by a 1-layer block looped L times with embedding size d+R+2 and R*H heads; Corollary 5.3: p-hop solved by looping 1 layer floor(log2 p)+2 times with O(log n) precision, matching the non-looped depth lower bound of Sanford et al.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.4: a looped transformer with L+O(1) layers and Omega(log(n+m)) extra embedding dimension simulates m CoT steps of an L-layer transformer using m loops over m appended dummy tokens.
claims.evidence_quote: the output of non-looped transformer after m steps of CoT, TFm θ (v), is the same as that of the looped transformer on input x concatenated by m dummy tokens with m loops

claims.claim: Downstream accuracy of both looped and deep models fits Acc = alpha log(D) + beta in effective depth D; loops help relatively more on reasoning tasks, and for reasoning primitives looping has larger slope than adding layers.

title: Think Shallow, Solve Deep: Controlling Recurrent Dynamics for Reliable Test-Time Depth
relevance_reason: Measures dynamical regime (settling/marginal/drifting) of weight-tied recurrent reasoners and links it to whether extra test-time iterations help; applies diagnostics to Huginn-3.5B.
one_sentence: Shows the finite-time dynamical regime of a trained recurrent operator (settling vs marginal vs drifting, via Lyapunov exponent) predicts whether extra test-time iterations help, proves a depth-safety condition, and shows a terminal fixed-point objective flips the regime.
key_contributions: Proposition 1: if remaining path length of the latent trajectory is below the decoder margin, the decoded answer can never change under further iterations (depth-safety); with infinite path length no finite constancy window certifies the answer (guess-freezing).

Four behavioral criteria (R1 extrapolation by iteration, R2 difficulty-adaptive stabilization, R3 incremental computation, R4 convergent answer) with a failure taxonomy across seven reimplemented recurrent architectures (TRM-style, UT/URM, FPRM, EqR, DEQ, Neural GPU, SE-RRM).

Causal lever: terminal fixed-point objective; removing it induces drift and removes gains, adding it to a generic recurrence yields depth-safe carry extrapolation; Huginn-3.5B measured as non-settling and repaired for depth-safety with a label-free LoRA objective.

setup.benchmarks: Sudoku 9x9 (hole fraction ladder), reachability (BFS depth 2-12, 16 nodes), 2x32-bit addition (carry length 2-28); maze/sorting/ARC as supporting

limitations: Tiny models and synthetic generators (Sudoku from one symmetry orbit); producing a settling operator is not guaranteed (seed lottery on mazes); conversion (gains from depth) remains empirical and task-dependent; Huginn repair is one checkpoint and operation-family scoped; finite-time Lyapunov estimates.
survey_notes: Important for the 'when does more test-time depth help' question: separates depth-safety (provable from measured settling) from conversion (empirical). Distinguishes size/length ladders (governed by size invariance) from fixed-size deeper-computation ladders; claims extrapolation only on the latter, which is a caution for reading length-generalization papers (2409.15647, 2606.29983) as evidence of 'thinking longer'. Agrees with 2202.05826 (removing recall collapses the operator to identity). Contradicts optimistic readings of Huginn test-time scaling: finds Huginn latent trajectories marginal and depth unsafe on procedural probes (cf. Lu et al. 2507.02199). Notes TRM fails without ~1000x augmentation under their protocol (0.00 on Sudoku), conflicting with TRM headline results that use augmentation.

title: Thinking Deeper, Not Longer: Memory-Efficient Test-Time Reasoning with Depth-Recurrent Transformers for Compositional Generalization
relevance_reason: Shared-weight recurrent block for compositional reasoning with final-only supervision, LayerScale and identity-biased gating; compares to fixed-depth, UT-ACT and CoT memory cost.
one_sentence: A sub-1M-parameter shared-weight recurrent transformer core, trained with final-step-only ('silent thinking') supervision, LayerScale and an identity-biased gate, extrapolates on graph reachability, nested boolean logic and relational text, while per-step supervision and ACT halting hurt extrapolation.
key_contributions: Recipe for stable 20+ step recurrence: silent thinking (loss only at final step), LayerScale init 1e-4, gated recurrence with gate bias -2.0 (gradient highway).

Computational frontier: accuracy jumps once thinking steps meet task depth; depth recurrence extrapolates on graphs where fixed-depth models collapse and matches fixed-depth transformers with 4-6.4x more parameters on sequence tasks.

Per-step (deep) supervision of the final answer induces shallow shortcuts and kills extrapolation; ACT Universal Transformer under-halts (~4 ponder steps) and returns to chance OOD; memory stays flat vs growing KV cache for CoT.

setup.model_sizes: shared-weight reasoning core under 1M parameters; d = 128/256/384 in supervision study
setup.train_tokens_or_data: synthetic graph reachability (train 1-5 hops), nested boolean logic, relational composition over shuffled text
setup.loops_train: externally specified step count T (e.g. up to 20 thinking steps)
setup.loops_test: larger T at test time; OOD hops 6-12 on graph
setup.baselines: fixed-depth Transformer, fixed-depth GNN, plain weight-tied block, Universal Transformer with ACT, intermediate-supervision variants
setup.benchmarks: graph reachability, nested boolean logic, relational (family) composition

claims.claim: Depth recurrence extrapolates on graph reachability where fixed-depth models barely extrapolate, and on sequence tasks comes within two points of fixed-depth transformers using 4-6.4x more parameters.
claims.regime: iso_param vs plain tied block; fixed-depth baselines have more params (unmatched)
claims.evidence_quote: it succeeds on the graph task where fixed-depth models barely extrapolate, and on the two sequence tasks comes within two points of fixed-depth Transformers that use 4–6.4× more parameters

claims.claim: Supervising the answer at every recurrence step (even with weight 0.1) makes the model learn shallow statistical shortcuts and destroys deep extrapolation; only final-step supervision solves 10-hop paths.
claims.evidence_quote: This property disappears even when α = 0.1: 10-hop accuracy falls to chance for every seed.

claims.claim: A Universal Transformer with ACT halting is the weakest recurrent variant: its learned halting saturates at about 4 ponder steps where 8-12 are needed, returning to chance beyond the training range.
claims.evidence_quote: its learned halting saturates at ≈4 ponder steps where 8–12 are structurally required and the ponder penalty rewards early stopping

numbers.quote: the fixed-depth Transformer extrapolates just one hop further (77% at 6 hops) before falling to chance at 8 hops and beyond
it solves 10-hop paths (84% at d = 256; 88–100% for all 5 seeds at d = 384)

numbers.quote: accuracy at depth 5 improves from 69.8% at 1 step to 81.7% at 12 steps

numbers.quote: it achieves roughly 65–70% accuracy on 12-hop paths after only a single thinking step

survey_notes: Assigned in theory_a under the shorter title 'Thinking Deeper, Not Longer: Depth-Recurrent Transformers for Compositional Generalization' with null id; resolved to 2603.21676 (full title contains both). Also on theory_b's list; dedupe on merge. Contradiction to record: per-step answer supervision hurts here, while 2510.14095 (step-specific algorithmic targets) and 2502.08482 (per-iteration CoT alignment) find per-step supervision helps; the difference is that here every step is supervised with the final answer (deep supervision), there each step has its own intermediate target. Also contrasts with deep-supervision recipes in TRM/HRM and 2608.18222 (4 supervised unrolls). ACT under-halting agrees with the general finding that learned halting can stabilize a suboptimal computation (2606.29983).
